title: Two Sum
statement: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to target. You may assume that each input has exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice. Return the answer in any order.
constraints: The same element may not be used twice

examples.explanation: 2 + 4 = 6. Note the answer is not [0, 2] because 3 + 3 is not 6.

hints.content: Before searching the whole array for a partner, what single piece of information would make the search instant?
For the current number x, you can compute exactly which number would complete the pair. Which one is it?
You need a structure that answers 'have I already seen this value, and at which index?' in average O(1). A HashMap does exactly that.
Use HashMap<Integer, Integer> seen. Check the complement BEFORE storing the current number, otherwise a single element could match itself.

pseudocode: for each index i with value x:
invariant: seen contains exactly the numbers already visited, mapped to the index where they were first seen.
whyThisPattern: The question is not 'find a pair in an array' but 'have I already seen the value I need?'. Once it is phrased that way, the answer is a HashMap lookup. The array is only scanned once, so each element costs O(1) and the total is O(n).
bruteForce: Check every pair: for i, for j > i, test nums[i] + nums[j] == target. That is O(n^2). At n = 100,000 it is about 5 * 10^9 comparisons, which is far too slow. Storing what you have seen turns it into n lookups.
interviewExplanation: I use a HashMap from value to index to remember the numbers I have already seen. For each number I compute the complement that would reach the target and check whether that complement is already in the map, which finds the pair in one pass. This gives O(n) time and O(n) space.
commonMistakes: Storing the current number before checking for the complement, which lets an element match itself.
Overwriting the index in the map instead of keeping the first one.
Trying to use two pointers on an unsorted array and sorting it, which loses the original indices.

options: An array of integers and one target integer
A stream of numbers with no target
breakdown.explanation: One array, nums, plus a single target. There is no second array to compare against, which is why the answer has to come from inside nums itself.

options: The two values that add up to the target
The indices of the two values that add up to the target
The count of pairs that add up to the target
Whether any pair adds up to the target
breakdown.explanation: Indices, not values. The problem is about positions, so anything that returns numbers instead of positions is answering a different question.

breakdown.prompt: Which constraint actually narrows the problem?
options: Exactly one answer exists, and you may not use the same element twice
breakdown.explanation: One answer and no self-matching element is the constraint that shapes the whole solution. It is why you look for the complement before you store the current number.
